entries.def: (= breaks the law and does something illegal/against the law/wrong)
entries.example: When someone commits a crime, the police do a number of things.

entries.def: (= try to find out what happened and who is responsible)

entries.example: If they catch the person they believe is responsible for the crime, they will arrest them.

entries.def: (= take them to the police station because they think the person has committed the crime)

entries.example: At the police station, they question them.

entries.def: (= the police make an official statement that they believe the person committed the crime)

entries.example: For a serious crime (e.g. murder), the person must then go to court for trial. (see section B)

entries.def: (= provide facts to show something is true)
entries.example: In court, the defendant must try to prove that they did not commit the crime.
Twelve members of the public (called the jury) listen to the evidence and then make their decision.

entries.def: (= information about the crime, for and against)

entries.example: People who see a crime are witnesses, and they usually give evidence at a trial.

entries.def: (= what a person must suffer if they do something wrong)

entries.example: If someone is guilty of a crime, the judge will give the sentence.
If a person is guilty of murder, the sentence may be 10–20 years in prison.
The person then becomes a prisoner.
For crimes that are not serious (called minor offences), the punishment is usually a fine.
